```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
set.seed(1)
```

`specdiv` turns *probabilistic* species predictions into per-site taxonomic,
phylogenetic and functional diversity that carries its own uncertainty. Instead
of committing each individual to a single identification and computing one
diversity number, it draws identities many times from a calibrated probability
vector, reconstitutes each site on every draw, and reports the mean and a
confidence interval for every axis — all three as Hill numbers of matched
order, a common "effective number of species" currency.

The engine does not care how the probabilities were produced. It was built for
nondestructive leaf-clip reflectance spectra of tree seedlings, and a spectral
front-end is provided for that case, but anything that emits a probability
matrix — imaging spectroscopy, camera-trap classifiers, metabarcoding
assignments — can drive it.

```{r setup}
library(specdiv)
library(ape)
```

## What you need

Three ingredients feed the engine:

1. a **probability matrix** `P` (rows = individuals, columns = species),
2. a **phylogeny** whose tip labels are those species (for the phylogenetic
   axis), and
3. a **functional distance matrix** among those species (for the functional
   axis).

Here we fabricate a tiny example. In practice `P` comes from your classifier
(see the spectral front-end below), the tree from `V.PhyloMaker2` or your own,
and the distances from measured traits via `trait_distance()`.

```{r toy-data}
species <- c("Acer", "Betula", "Corylus", "Fraxinus")

# a phylogeny (tip labels must match the species columns of P)
tree <- read.tree(text = "((Acer:1,Betula:1):1,(Corylus:1,Fraxinus:1):1);")

# a functional distance matrix from two standardised traits
traits <- rbind(Acer     = c(lma = 60, succ = 0.9),
                Betula   = c(lma = 55, succ = 1.0),
                Corylus  = c(lma = 90, succ = 0.6),
                Fraxinus = c(lma = 85, succ = 0.7))
Dfun <- trait_distance(traits)

# 40 individuals across 4 sites, with a per-individual probability vector.
n <- 40
site  <- rep(1:4, each = 10)
truth <- sample(species, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.4, .3, .2, .1))

# a mock "classifier": mostly-right probabilities, sharper for some individuals
P <- matrix(0.05, n, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, species))
for (i in seq_len(n)) P[i, truth[i]] <- runif(1, 0.5, 0.95)
P <- P / rowSums(P)
head(round(P, 2))
```

## Calibrating the probabilities

The probabilities are *sampled from*, so they must be honest: a stated 80%
confidence should be right about 80% of the time. If you have cross-validated
predictions and their true labels, `fit_temperature()` finds a one-parameter
power scaling that matches mean confidence to accuracy, and `temperature_scale()`
applies it.

```{r calibrate}
ft <- fit_temperature(P, truth)          # here P doubles as its own CV set
ft$gamma
P_cal <- temperature_scale(P, ft$gamma)
```

## Diversity with uncertainty

`propagate_diversity()` is the core call. Give it the probabilities, the site
of each individual, and (optionally) the tree and functional distances. With
`truth` supplied it also returns the census-based `true_*` columns, so you can
validate.

```{r propagate}
div <- propagate_diversity(
  P_cal, site,
  tree = tree, trait_dist = Dfun, truth = truth,
  q = c(0, 1, 2), n_draws = 300, seed = 1
)
round(div[, c("site", "n_seedlings",
              "TD1", "TD1_lo", "TD1_hi", "true_TD1",
              "PD1", "true_PD1", "FD1", "true_FD1")], 2)
```

Each metric is named by axis (`TD` taxonomic, `PD` phylogenetic, `FD`
functional) and order (`0`, `1`, `2`), with `_lo`/`_hi` giving the 95%
Monte Carlo interval. A quick validation plot of the Shannon (q = 1) taxonomic
axis against the census truth:

```{r validate-plot, fig.alt = "Spectra-derived vs census diversity"}
with(div, {
  plot(true_TD1, TD1, pch = 19, xlab = "Census diversity",
       ylab = "Predicted diversity", xlim = range(c(true_TD1, TD1_lo, TD1_hi)),
       ylim = range(c(true_TD1, TD1_lo, TD1_hi)))
  arrows(true_TD1, TD1_lo, true_TD1, TD1_hi, length = 0, col = "grey")
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
})
```

## Assemblage structure (clustering vs overdispersion)

`ses_structure()` propagates the same uncertainty into standardized effect
sizes of mean pairwise (MPD) and mean nearest-taxon distance (MNTD), on both
axes, using **picante**. Negative values mean co-occurring individuals are more
related / more similar than chance (clustering). This needs the `picante`
package, so it is not evaluated here:

```{r ses, eval = FALSE}
ses <- ses_structure(P_cal, site, tree = tree, trait_dist = Dfun,
                     truth = truth, n_draws = 200, runs = 499, seed = 1)
ses[, c("site", "pMPD_ses", "pMPD_lo", "pMPD_hi", "fMPD_ses")]
```

## The spectral front-end

For the leaf-spectroscopy case, the package supplies the steps that produce `P`
from raw spectra. Preprocess identically for training and deployment, fit a
PLS-DA classifier (via **mixOmics**), and predict probabilities:

```{r spectral, eval = FALSE}
Xtr <- preprocess_spectra(train_spectra, "deriv")   # SNV + 1st derivative
Xte <- preprocess_spectra(plot_spectra,  "deriv")

model <- fit_spectral_classifier(Xtr, train_species, ncomp = 24)
P_raw <- predict_probs(model, Xte)

# calibrate on cross-validated reference predictions, then propagate as above
```

Two deployment levers matter in practice, and both have helpers:

- **Cross-campaign transfer.** A library ages: predicting a later season from an
  earlier one transfers poorly. `batch_align(new_x, ref_x)` removes a global
  batch offset; better still, re-anchor the library with a small same-season
  re-scan.
- **Open species pool.** Assuming the species present is powerful but often
  impossible. Train a broad library and apply `apply_abundance_prior(P, counts)`,
  where `counts` can be an independent, scan-free survey of a second set of
  sites — it recovers most of the closed-set accuracy.

```{r levers, eval = FALSE}
P_aligned <- predict_probs(model, batch_align(Xte, Xtr))
P_post    <- apply_abundance_prior(P_raw, independent_counts)
```

## Summary

The load-bearing idea is that prediction is uncertain, and a diversity number
computed from hard classifications hides that. `specdiv` keeps the uncertainty
in view from the first probability to the final interval, and reports all three
diversity axes in one currency so they can be read side by side.
